overview.introduction: This lecture introduces Political Economy as a field and examines corruption as its first applied case. Political Economy studies how political constraints — arising from conflicts of interest — shape economic policy and outcomes. Corruption serves as the perfect opening example: it shows how institutional weaknesses distort economic outcomes.
keyTakeaways: Political Economy = how political constraints cause policies to diverge from the social optimum
Heterogeneity (conflict of interest) is the defining feature — without it, there is no political problem
Corruption is an institutional OUTCOME, not an exogenous shock — it reflects weak institutions
Micro evidence on corruption costs is stronger than macro evidence (e.g. Uganda: only 13% of school grants arrived)
Transparency and citizen monitoring work better than higher wages or more competition

sections.heading: What is Political Economy?
sections.content: Political Economy studies how collective choice mechanisms (voting, bargaining, lobbying) resolve conflicts of interest and determine economic policy. It differs from welfare economics (which takes the SWF as given), public finance (which assumes optimal taxes), and public choice (which studies decision mechanisms without focusing on macro effects). The key insight: politics is not a friction to be removed, it IS the mechanism through which policy is made.

sections.heading: Why Heterogeneity Matters
sections.content: Without conflict of interests, there is no political problem — a representative agent would just implement the optimal policy. Drazen distinguishes ex-ante heterogeneity (different preferences/endowments) from ex-post heterogeneity (identical agents fighting over distribution). Both create political problems that push outcomes away from the social optimum.

sections.heading: Corruption: The First Application
sections.content: Svensson defines corruption as misuse of public office for private gain. It is correlated with low income, weak institutions, closed economies, and low press freedom. The magnitude is enormous: in Uganda, 80% of firms paid bribes and only 13% of school grants reached schools. Higher wages and competition have ambiguous effects — transparency and reducing discretion work better.

sections.heading: Two Ways Politics Distorts Outcomes
sections.content: Even when political bargaining reaches a Pareto-efficient point, society may prefer a different one (bias). Additionally, the political process uses real resources, leading to outcomes off the contract curve entirely (inefficiency). This framework explains delayed stabilisations, political business cycles, deficit bias, and corruption.

keyTerms.definition: Study of how political constraints (conflict + collective choice) cause actual policies to diverge from optimal policies
Conflict of interests — the necessary condition for PE. Can be ex-ante (different preferences) or ex-post (distributional conflict)
Misuse of public office for private gain. An institutional outcome, not an exogenous shock
Hypothetical benevolent dictator who implements optimal policy — PE rejects this assumption
Positive: explains why policies diverge from optimum. Normative: designs institutions to overcome political constraints

Conflict of interests — the necessary condition for political economy to exist
Agents enter politics with different preferences, endowments, or beliefs
Identical agents with distributional conflict over dividing a given pie
Political process selects the wrong point on the Pareto frontier
Political process uses real resources, pushing outcomes off the Pareto frontier entirely
Explains WHY actual policies diverge from the social optimum
Designs institutions to overcome political constraints and improve outcomes
Welfare econ takes SWF weights as given; PE endogenises them — politics determines the weights
Public choice studies decision mechanisms per se; PE focuses on their macroeconomic effects
Misuse of public office for private gain — an institutional outcome, not an exogenous shock
Corruption = direct transfer (bribe); Rent-seeking = socially costly pursuit of rents
Lobbying = collective, permanent, legal; Corruption = individual, transitory, illegal
Reversible, low-commitment production adopted by firms facing corruption — easy to abandon if extorted
Idea that corruption helps bypass bad regulation — Svensson rejects this
Giving citizens information to monitor officials and demand accountability
Hypothetical benevolent dictator implementing optimal policy — PE rejects this as unrealistic

questions.question: How does political economy differ from welfare economics in analyzing policy?
questions.explanation: Political economy explicitly incorporates political constraints from heterogeneity and conflict, whereas welfare economics takes the social welfare function as given.

Ex-post determines initial preferences while ex-ante creates institutional weaknesses

questions.question: What distinguishes ex-ante from ex-post heterogeneity in political economy?
questions.explanation: Ex-ante heterogeneity involves different preferences before uncertainty resolves, while ex-post heterogeneity describes distributional conflict that emerges after outcomes occur.

questions.question: Which two distortions can result from political constraints on economic policy?
questions.explanation: Political constraints create two types of distortions: bias (choosing wrong Pareto point) and inefficiency (operating off the production frontier entirely).
